```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source(file.path("R", "helpers.R"))
invisible(set_project_root())
check_required_packages()
configure_pandoc()
source(file.path("R", "01_data_cleaning.R"))
source(file.path("R", "02_eda_visualizations.R"))
source(file.path("R", "03_statistical_analysis.R"))

cleaned <- read_clean_data()
station_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/station_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
daily_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/daily_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
hourly_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/hourly_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
monthly_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/monthly_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seasonal_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/seasonal_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
holiday_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/holiday_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cleaning_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/cleaning_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
station_coverage <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/station_coverage_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
descriptive <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/descriptive_statistics.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
comparison <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/weekday_weekend_test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
coefficients <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/regression_coefficients.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
model_summary <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/regression_model_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
assumption_checks <- readr::read_csv("outputs/tables/regression_assumption_checks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

peak_hour <- hourly_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_max(.data$mean_passengers_per_observed_hour, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
highest_station <- station_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_max(.data$total_passengers, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
lowest_station <- station_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_min(.data$total_passengers, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
peak_month <- monthly_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_max(.data$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
lowest_month <- monthly_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_min(.data$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
peak_season <- seasonal_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_max(.data$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
lowest_season <- seasonal_summary |>
  dplyr::slice_min(.data$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
holiday_means <- holiday_summary |>
  dplyr::select(holiday, mean_daily_station_passengers)
holiday_mean <- stats::setNames(
  holiday_means$mean_daily_station_passengers,
  as.character(holiday_means$holiday)
)
weekend_coefficient <- coefficients |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$term == "weekend")
holiday_coefficient <- coefficients |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$term == "holiday_indicator")
```

# Introduction

Public transportation ridership varies by station, time of day, day of week,
and season. Understanding these patterns helps describe when and where transit
service is most heavily used. This project examines a real hourly ridership
extract from the New York City Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA).
The analysis describes patterns in the selected station sample; it does not
estimate causal effects.

# Objectives

- Clean and validate dated station-level passenger and transfer counts.
- Describe station, hourly, weekday/weekend, monthly, and holiday patterns.
- Visualize the relationships and summarize them with transparent statistical
  tests and a regression model.
- Save reusable cleaned data, tables, charts, and this report automatically.

# Dataset description and source

The data comes from the MTA's official **Subway Hourly Ridership: 2020-2024**
dataset, available through the [NYC Open Data dataset page](https://data.ny.gov/Transportation/MTA-Subway-Hourly-Ridership-2020-2024/wujg-7c2s)
and the [Socrata CSV API](https://data.ny.gov/resource/wujg-7c2s.csv).
The extract in this project covers January 1 through December 31, 2024, and
contains timestamps, station-complex IDs and names, boroughs, passenger
counts, and transfer counts. Fare/payment categories are summed into one
passenger and transfer total per station-hour.

To keep this beginner project practical to download and run, it follows ten
station complexes throughout the year: five high- and five low-ridership
stations in the January 2, 2024 snapshot of the MTA data. These were chosen
using that date's station totals; the sample is not a random or exhaustive
sample of all NYC stations. The station selection means demand rankings and
findings apply to these ten stations only.

The timestamps are published as local NYC wall-clock times without a UTC
offset. The workflow parses the text without converting the displayed hour,
so the hour-of-day analysis follows the source's clock values.

```{r data-overview}
knitr::kable(
  tibble::tibble(
    Item = c("Cleaned station-hour records", "Stations", "Date range",
             "Passenger field", "Operational field"),
    Value = c(
      nrow(cleaned),
      dplyr::n_distinct(cleaned$station_id),
      paste(min(cleaned$date), "to", max(cleaned$date)),
      "MTA ridership total by station-hour",
      "MTA transfer total by station-hour"
    )
  ),
  caption = "Overview of the cleaned analysis dataset"
)
```

# Preprocessing

The cleaning script standardizes column names, parses timestamps and counts,
removes rows with invalid required values, limits records to 2024, and removes
duplicate station/timestamp records. Missing or negative passenger/transfer
counts are not imputed: invalid records are excluded so fabricated ridership
is not introduced. The source API aggregation produces one row per station
complex and timestamp. Extreme passenger counts are flagged using a
high-tail IQR rule and retained because large peaks can be valid observations.
The public extract does not contain every possible station-hour. Missing
station-hour records are not converted to zero or imputed; consequently,
partial-day totals are not comparable with complete days. The weekday/weekend
test, weekday/weekend box plot, and holiday summaries use only station-days
with all 24 hourly observations. Cleaning and coverage counts are calculated
by the script:

```{r cleaning-summary}
knitr::kable(cleaning_summary, caption = "Cleaning and validation summary")
knitr::kable(
  station_coverage,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Observed versus expected station-hour coverage"
)
```

# Exploratory data analysis

## Station demand

```{r station-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/01_station_demand.png")
```

The bars rank the ten sampled station complexes by total observed 2024
passengers. The highest and lowest names and totals in this selected sample
are **`r highest_station$station`** (`r scales::comma(round(highest_station$total_passengers))`)
and **`r lowest_station$station`** (`r scales::comma(round(lowest_station$total_passengers))`),
respectively. This ranking should not be interpreted as a citywide ranking.
The station coverage table in Preprocessing shows how many station-hours were
reported for each station; annual totals at stations with less coverage are
not directly comparable as if all stations had complete records.

## Daily demand trend

```{r trend-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/02_daily_demand_trend.png")
```

The line shows mean passengers per reported station-hour for each date, rather
than a daily total, so it is less affected by the number of records that day.
The orange smooth line helps reveal broad changes over time; one-day peaks may
reflect special events, service conditions, or reporting variation and are not
explained by this observational analysis.

## Peak passenger hours

```{r hourly-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/03_hourly_demand.png")
```

The highest mean in the hourly profile occurs at **`r peak_hour$hour`:00**
(`r round(peak_hour$mean_passengers_per_observed_hour, 1)` passengers per
reported station-hour). This compares hours using an average rather than a
total that could be affected by unequal reporting coverage.

## Weekday and hour pattern

```{r heatmap, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/04_weekday_hour_heatmap.png")
```

The heat map compares mean station-hour counts by weekday and clock hour.
Brighter cells indicate higher average observed counts and help identify
whether peak hours differ across weekdays.

## Weekday versus weekend demand

```{r weekday-weekend-chart, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/05_weekday_weekend_boxplot.png")
```

The box plot displays only station-days with all 24 hourly records. This avoids
comparing partial days as though they were complete; station sample sizes
differ substantially because the source has uneven coverage.

## Monthly and seasonal demand

```{r monthly-chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/06_monthly_demand.png")
```

Mean passengers per reported station-hour vary by month. In this sample the
highest-average month is
**`r as.character(peak_month$month_name)`**
(`r round(peak_month$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, 1)`), and the
lowest-average month is **`r as.character(lowest_month$month_name)`**
(`r round(lowest_month$mean_passengers_per_station_hour, 1)`). A single
year's monthly pattern does not establish a recurring seasonal effect.

```{r monthly-seasonal-tables}
knitr::kable(
  monthly_summary,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Monthly ridership totals and average observed station-hour counts"
)
knitr::kable(
  seasonal_summary,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Seasonal ridership totals and average observed station-hour counts"
)
```

Grouping calendar months into three-month seasons, the largest total is
observed in **`r as.character(peak_season$season)`** and the smallest in
**`r as.character(lowest_season$season)`**. Winter combines January, February,
and December within the 2024 extract. These averages describe this one year
and do not establish a recurring annual cycle.

## Holiday-related demand

The holiday indicator uses the 2024 U.S. federal holiday calendar added during
preprocessing; it is not a holiday field supplied by the MTA. Holiday
observations are few, so their comparison is descriptive only.

```{r holiday-chart, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/07_holiday_comparison.png")
```

The holiday chart compares complete station-days only. The mean daily station
count is `r scales::comma(round(holiday_mean[["Holiday"]]))` on identified
federal holidays and `r scales::comma(round(holiday_mean[["Non-holiday"]]))`
on other dates. Holiday observations are relatively few, so the difference is
descriptive and should not be generalized to other years.

```{r holiday-table}
knitr::kable(
  holiday_summary,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Daily station-count summaries on holiday and non-holiday dates"
)
```

## Relationships among recorded variables

The passenger/transfer correlation across station-hour records is
`r round(descriptive$passenger_transfer_correlation, 3)`. These are related
operational counts from the same station-hours, and correlation does not show
that transfers cause ridership or vice versa.

```{r relationship-chart, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
knitr::include_graphics("outputs/plots/08_passengers_transfers_relationship.png")
```

Each panel shows the relationship within one station, reducing the visual
confounding caused by differences in overall station size. The fitted line
describes association only.

# Statistical analysis

## Descriptive statistics

```{r descriptive-table}
knitr::kable(
  descriptive,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Descriptive statistics for station-hour records"
)
```

## Weekday/weekend comparison test

The comparison uses the **paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test** on each station's
mean daily weekday count and mean daily weekend count, using only complete
24-hour station-days. Pairing controls for
the large baseline differences between stations. The analysis includes
`r comparison$paired_stations` stations that have complete observations for
both day types; the test assumes those station pairs are independent and the
distribution of paired differences is reasonably symmetric. A Shapiro-Wilk
test of paired differences is included as a diagnostic, not as proof of
normality.

```{r comparison-table}
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4, caption = "Paired weekday/weekend test")
```

The estimated paired median difference (weekday minus weekend) is
`r scales::comma(round(comparison$median_paired_difference_weekday_minus_weekend))`
passengers per station-day. The Wilcoxon p-value is
`r format.pval(comparison$p_value, digits = 3)`. This test assesses evidence
of a difference among the selected stations; it does not establish why any
difference occurs.

## Regression model and assumption checks

An ordinary least-squares model predicts `log(1 + passengers)` from weekend
status, the holiday indicator, hour, month, and station-complex fixed effects.
The log transformation reduces right-skew; categorical time and station
terms adjust for recurring hour/month patterns and baseline station scale.
This is an explanatory association model, not a causal model. Standard OLS
errors assume independent observations and an adequately specified conditional
mean and variance structure; hourly observations can be serially correlated
and heteroskedastic, so conventional p-values may be too optimistic.

```{r model-assumption-checks}
knitr::kable(
  assumption_checks,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Numeric checks of residual normality and spread"
)
```

The residual standard deviations across fitted-value quartiles help flag
uneven spread; the Shapiro-Wilk test checks a reproducible residual sample.
Neither replaces a visual diagnostic, and hourly dependence remains a
limitation of the model.

```{r model-summary}
knitr::kable(
  model_summary |>
    dplyr::select(
      r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma, statistic, p.value, df, nobs
    ),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Overall ordinary least-squares model summary"
)
```

```{r model-key-coefficients}
key_terms <- dplyr::bind_rows(weekend_coefficient, holiday_coefficient) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    term = dplyr::recode(
      .data$term,
      weekend = "Weekend versus weekday",
      holiday_indicator = "Federal holiday versus non-holiday"
    )
  )
knitr::kable(
  key_terms |>
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Key adjusted associations on the log(1 + passenger count) scale"
)
```

The weekend and holiday coefficients describe adjusted associations on the
log-transformed outcome scale, holding the model's station, hour, and month
terms constant. They should not be read as causal effects or as exact
percentage changes in raw passenger counts.

# Findings

- Within the selected sample, **`r highest_station$station`** has the largest
  total and **`r lowest_station$station`** the smallest.
- The sample's busiest clock hour is **`r peak_hour$hour`:00**.
- The highest and lowest monthly mean passenger rates occur in
  **`r as.character(peak_month$month_name)`** and
  **`r as.character(lowest_month$month_name)`**, respectively.
- The highest seasonal mean rate occurs in **`r as.character(peak_season$season)`**.
- The paired weekday/weekend comparison gives a median station difference of
  `r scales::comma(round(comparison$median_paired_difference_weekday_minus_weekend))`
  weekday passengers per station-day and a p-value of
  `r format.pval(comparison$p_value, digits = 3)`.

# Recommendations

- Use the hourly and weekday-hour patterns as an initial guide for further
  service-planning review, then validate them against a full-network extract
  and actual service schedules.
- Investigate the highest and lowest observed station patterns alongside
  local population, service changes, disruptions, and special events before
  making operational decisions.
- Repeat the monthly and holiday analysis across multiple years and include
  service-supply, event, and weather information before interpreting changes.

# Limitations

- The analysis follows ten deliberately selected station complexes, not all
  stations; the sample is not statistically representative of the network.
- A single calendar year cannot establish long-term trends or recurring
  seasonality.
- Holiday flags come from a manually specified federal holiday calendar.
  Transit ridership may respond differently to holidays, observed dates, and
  nearby school or local holidays.
- Missing or invalid counts are excluded rather than imputed. Extreme but
  nonnegative counts are retained and flagged.
- Ridership and transfers are observational counts. Unmeasured service
  changes, disruptions, and external conditions may influence both.
- The regression uses conventional OLS standard errors despite the potential
  for serial dependence and heteroskedasticity in hourly counts.

# Conclusion

This reproducible workflow cleans the public MTA ridership extract, generates
ten figures and reusable summary/model tables, tests a paired weekday/weekend
difference, and fits a log-linear OLS model. Its results describe temporal
and station-level patterns in a small selected sample. A full-network,
multi-year analysis with stronger time-series and service-context modeling
would be needed before making network-wide or causal claims.
